osces.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome - STEMI Management
osces.scenario: You are the emergency physician on call. A 58-year-old male plumber presents to ED with sudden-onset severe central chest pain that started 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy pipes at work. The pain is crushing in nature, radiates to his left arm and jaw, and is associated with diaphoresis and nausea. He has a history of hypertension and is a current smoker (30 pack-years). His wife drove him to hospital immediately. Vital signs: BP 145/90, HR 95, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 36.8°C. He appears pale and diaphoretic.

patient_presentation.chief_complaint: Severe crushing central chest pain for 45 minutes
patient_presentation.history: 58-year-old male plumber with sudden-onset severe central chest pain while lifting heavy equipment. Pain is 9/10, crushing, radiates to left arm and jaw. Associated with diaphoresis, nausea, and feeling of impending doom. No previous episodes. Current smoker 30 pack-years. Takes amlodipine 10mg daily for hypertension. No known allergies.
patient_presentation.examination_findings: Appears distressed, pale, diaphoretic. Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs. JVP not elevated. No peripheral oedema. Chest: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. Peripheral pulses present and equal.

ecg.findings: Sinus rhythm at 95 bpm. ST elevation 4mm in leads II, III, aVF. Reciprocal ST depression 2mm in leads I, aVL. Q waves not yet present. QT interval 420ms (normal).
ecg.interpretation: Acute inferior STEMI - likely RCA occlusion

investigations.chest_xray: Normal heart size, clear lung fields, no acute pathology

management_tasks.details: Give aspirin 300mg PO stat, ticagrelor 180mg PO stat loading dose, atorvastatin 80mg PO stat. Commence IV access and continuous cardiac monitoring.
Door-to-balloon time target <90 minutes. Contact interventional cardiology team immediately. If PCI not available within 90 minutes, consider thrombolysis with tenecteplase.
Commence enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC BD or bivalirudin if going for primary PCI. Avoid unfractionated heparin due to bleeding risk.
Morphine 2.5mg IV PRN for pain relief. Metoprolol 25mg BD PO once haemodynamically stable. Monitor for complications (arrhythmias, heart failure, mechanical complications).

clinical_reasoning.significance: Supports single vessel disease pattern typical of proximal RCA occlusion

clinical_reasoning.interpretation: Confirms myocardial necrosis consistent with STEMI

osces.title: Heart Failure Assessment and Management
osces.scenario: Mrs Jennifer Walsh, a 72-year-old retired teacher, presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion but now present at rest. She reports orthopnoea requiring 3 pillows to sleep, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea twice in the past week, and bilateral ankle swelling. She has a past medical history of anterior STEMI 2 years ago treated with primary PCI and stent to LAD, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metoprolol 50mg BD, perindopril 8mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg nocte, and metformin 1000mg BD. On examination, she appears dyspnoeic at rest, with elevated JVP to angle of jaw, bilateral fine inspiratory crackles to mid-zones, and 2+ pitting oedema to mid-shins bilaterally.

patient_demographics.presentation: Progressive dyspnoea with signs of fluid overload

learning_objectives: Assess and classify heart failure severity using NYHA functional class

clinical_tasks.instructions: Elicit symptoms of heart failure, assess functional capacity, identify precipitating factors, and review current medications and adherence
key_points: NYHA functional class assessment - patient reports inability to climb stairs without stopping (Class III)
Orthopnoea requiring 3 pillows and PND episodes indicate volume overload
Previous STEMI with reduced ejection fraction as underlying cause
Medication adherence - patient admits to occasionally missing perindopril doses
No recent chest pain, fever, or medication changes

clinical_tasks.instructions: Conduct systematic examination focusing on signs of heart failure and volume status assessment
key_points: Elevated JVP to angle of jaw indicates elevated right heart pressures
Displaced apex beat laterally suggesting cardiomegaly
S3 gallop rhythm present on cardiac auscultation
Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles to mid-zones indicating pulmonary oedema
2+ pitting oedema to mid-shins bilaterally confirming volume overload

clinical_tasks.instructions: Review provided echo report and explain findings relevant to heart failure diagnosis and management
key_points: Left ventricular ejection fraction 35% indicating reduced systolic function
Global hypokinesis with akinesis of anterior and septal walls consistent with previous LAD territory infarct
Left ventricular end-diastolic diameter 6.2cm indicating chamber dilatation
Moderate mitral regurgitation secondary to papillary muscle dysfunction
No significant valvular stenosis or pericardial disease

clinical_tasks.instructions: Optimize medical therapy according to Australian Heart Foundation guidelines with specific doses and PBS codes
key_points: Increase perindopril to 10mg daily (maximum tolerated dose) - PBS 8254Q
Add bisoprolol 1.25mg daily, titrate gradually to target 10mg daily - PBS 8637M
Commence spironolactone 25mg daily (eGFR >60, K+ 4.2mmol/L) - PBS 2119B
Frusemide 40mg daily for symptomatic relief of fluid overload - PBS 2900Q
Continue atorvastatin 40mg nocte - existing therapy appropriate

clinical_tasks.instructions: Discuss immediate treatment, monitoring requirements, lifestyle modifications and specialist referral indications
key_points: Admission for IV diuretics and close monitoring of electrolytes and renal function
Daily weights and fluid restriction to 1.5L per day during admission
Cardiology referral for consideration of ICD therapy (EF <35% despite optimal medical therapy)
Heart failure nurse specialist referral for education and ongoing support
Follow-up with GP in 1 week post-discharge with repeat UEC and medication titration plan

scenario.chief_complaint: Increasing shortness of breath and ankle swelling over the past 2 weeks

history.presenting_illness: Mrs Chen presents with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnoea, initially on exertion but now occurring at rest. She reports orthopnoea (requiring 3 pillows to sleep) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea occurring twice this week. She has noticed bilateral ankle swelling and her shoes no longer fit. She denies chest pain but reports fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. Previously able to walk 500m, now struggles with 50m on flat ground.
history.social_history: Non-smoker, minimal alcohol consumption, lives independently with husband

examination_findings.general_appearance: Appears dyspnoeic at rest, sitting upright, mild distress

cardiovascular.inspection: Visible jugular venous distension at 45 degrees (8cm above sternal angle)
cardiovascular.palpation: Apex beat displaced laterally to 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. Weak peripheral pulses.
cardiovascular.auscultation: S1 and S2 heart sounds present. Soft S3 gallop heard at apex. Grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla.

respiratory.percussion: Dullness to percussion at both lung bases
respiratory.auscultation: Fine bibasal crackles extending to mid-zones bilaterally

examination_findings.abdominal: Mild hepatomegaly (liver edge 2cm below right costal margin), no ascites
examination_findings.extremities: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shins, cool peripheries

specific_changes: Poor R wave progression V1-V3 (Q waves in V2-V4 consistent with old anterior MI)
Left ventricular hypertrophy criteria present (S in V1 + R in V5 = 45mm)
T wave inversion in V5-V6, I, aVL

investigations.chest_xray: Enlarged cardiac silhouette (cardiothoracic ratio 0.65), bilateral lower lobe alveolar shadowing consistent with pulmonary oedema, small bilateral pleural effusions

blood_tests.troponin_i: 25 ng/L (elevated, consistent with acute heart failure)

investigations.echocardiogram: Severely impaired left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 25%). Regional wall motion abnormalities in anterior and septal walls. Moderate functional mitral regurgitation. Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 55mmHg.

expected_actions: Auscultate for S3 gallop and murmurs
Recognize evidence of previous anterior MI (Q waves V2-V4)
Comment on T wave changes suggesting ischaemia/strain
Classify as HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
Identify precipitating factors (medication non-compliance, dietary indiscretion)
Monitor fluid balance and daily weights
Consider IV nitrates for preload reduction

acute_management.details: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen 6L/min to maintain SpO2 >95%

acute_management.medication: Furosemide 80mg IV stat, then 40mg IV BD - PBS 2124Y
acute_management.monitoring: Hourly urine output, daily weights, electrolytes 12-hourly

acute_management.medication: Glyceryl trinitrate 10-20mcg/min IV infusion (if SBP >100mmHg) - PBS 1458F
acute_management.monitoring: Continuous BP monitoring, titrate to symptom relief

acute_management.details: Temporarily reduce ramipril to 5mg daily due to renal impairment, restart at full dose when creatinine stabilises

chronic_management.medication: Ramipril 10mg daily (when renal function stable) - PBS 8254G
chronic_management.rationale: ACE inhibitor - proven mortality benefit in HFrEF

chronic_management.medication: Carvedilol 6.25mg BD, titrate to 25mg BD - PBS 8427M
chronic_management.rationale: Beta-blocker with proven mortality benefit, replace metoprolol
Aldosterone antagonist for NYHA III-IV HF, monitor K+ and creatinine

follow_up: Cardiology outpatient review in 2 weeks
Heart failure nurse clinic appointment in 1 week
Repeat echocardiogram in 3 months to assess response
Consider cardiac rehabilitation program
Dietitian review for sodium restriction (<2g daily)

osces.title: ECG Interpretation - Inferior STEMI with Right Heart Extension
osces.instructions: A 58-year-old male presents to ED with sudden-onset severe central chest pain radiating to the jaw, occurring 90 minutes ago while gardening. The patient appears diaphoretic and nauseated. Vital signs: BP 95/60, HR 55 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air. You are the cardiology registrar called to interpret his ECG and initiate immediate management.

patient_background.presenting_complaint: Sudden-onset severe central chest pain with jaw radiation, onset 90 minutes ago during gardening activity
patient_background.medical_history: Hypertension (diagnosed 5 years ago), dyslipidaemia, ex-smoker (quit 2 years ago, 30-pack-year history), no known CAD
patient_background.family_history: Father died of MI aged 62, mother has T2DM

physical_examination.general: Appears distressed, diaphoretic, pale, clutching chest
physical_examination.cardiovascular: JVP elevated to 8cm, S3 gallop present, soft systolic murmur at LLSB, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented, no focal deficits

specific_changes.inferior_leads: ST elevation 4mm in leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression 2mm in leads I and aVL
specific_changes.right_sided_leads: ST elevation 3mm in V3R and V4R indicating RV involvement
specific_changes.posterior_leads: Tall R waves in V1-V2 with R/S ratio >1, suggesting posterior wall involvement
specific_changes.q_waves: Pathological Q waves 40ms width in leads III and aVF

assessment_tasks.instructions: Systematically interpret the 12-lead ECG. Identify the territory of infarction and any complications.
expected_findings: ST elevation 4mm in leads II, III, aVF indicating inferior STEMI
Reciprocal ST depression 2mm in leads I and aVL
Right heart involvement evidenced by ST elevation 3mm in V3R and V4R
Posterior wall involvement suggested by tall R waves in V1-V2 with R/S ratio >1
Pathological Q waves in leads III and aVF indicating established myocardial necrosis

assessment_tasks.instructions: Assess the patient's haemodynamic status and identify complications of acute MI.
expected_findings: Hypotension (95/60) suggesting cardiogenic shock or RV dysfunction
Bradycardia consistent with inferior MI affecting RCA and AV node
Signs of heart failure: S3 gallop, bibasal crepitations, elevated JVP
RV dysfunction evidenced by elevated JVP and systolic murmur at LLSB

immediate_actions.action: Call Code STEMI and activate catheter lab
immediate_actions.rationale: Door-to-balloon target <90 minutes for primary PCI

immediate_actions.details: Two large-bore IV cannulae, continuous cardiac monitoring

immediate_actions.rationale: Assess LV function and exclude mechanical complications

medications.contraindications: Use cautiously given bradycardia and hypotension

medications.rationale: Anticoagulation therapy, adjust for renal function

considerations: RV dysfunction may require specific management during PCI
Consider temporary pacing wire given bradycardia and AV conduction risk
Posterior wall involvement may require additional vessel intervention

Complete heart block - prepare for temporary pacing
RV failure - avoid preload reduction, consider dobutamine
Mechanical complications - papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture

osces.title: ECG Interpretation - Inferior STEMI

scenario.presentation: A 58-year-old builder presents to ED with sudden onset severe central chest pain radiating to left arm, started 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy materials at work. Pain described as crushing, 9/10 severity, associated with nausea, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath. No relief with rest.
scenario.history: Past medical history: Hypertension (on amlodipine), dyslipidaemia (on atorvastatin), ex-smoker (quit 2 years ago, 30 pack-year history). Family history of IHD - father had MI at age 62. No known allergies. Takes amlodipine 5mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg nocte.

ecg_findings.morphology_changes: ST elevation 4-5mm in leads II, III, aVF. Lead III shows greater ST elevation than lead II. Reciprocal ST depression 2mm in leads I and aVL. T waves upright and prominent in inferior leads.
ecg_findings.lead_analysis: Lead I: ST depression 2mm, T wave inversion. Lead II: ST elevation 4mm, tall T waves. Lead III: ST elevation 5mm, tall T waves. aVF: ST elevation 4mm. aVL: ST depression 2mm, T wave inversion. V1-V6: No acute changes, normal R wave progression.

tasks.details: Use systematic approach: Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals (PR, QRS, QT), then morphology analysis including P waves, QRS complexes, ST segments, and T waves. Measure ST elevation precisely using calipers.

tasks.instruction: Provide your diagnosis and explain the ECG changes
tasks.details: State primary diagnosis as acute ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) - inferior territory. Explain coronary anatomy: RCA supplies inferior wall (leads II, III, aVF). Reciprocal changes in leads I, aVL indicate transmural infarction.

Activate STEMI pathway, aim for door-to-balloon <90 minutes. Dual antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, symptom control. Discuss primary PCI vs thrombolysis based on local protocols and contraindications.

clinical_findings.inspection: Patient appears distressed, diaphoretic, pale. No peripheral oedema or cyanosis. JVP not elevated at 45 degrees.
clinical_findings.palpation: Pulse 76/min regular, good volume. Blood pressure 158/94 mmHg bilateral. Apex beat palpable 5th intercostal space midclavicular line, not displaced.
clinical_findings.auscultation: Heart sounds I and II normal, no murmurs, rubs or gallops heard. Chest clear to auscultation bilaterally.

investigations.indication: Confirm myocardial necrosis in context of STEMI
investigations.expected_result: Elevated >99th percentile (>26 ng/L), likely significantly elevated given clinical presentation

investigations.test: Full blood count, UEC, LFTs, lipids, glucose, coagulation studies
investigations.indication: Baseline investigations before anticoagulation and to assess comorbidities
investigations.expected_result: May show leucocytosis as stress response, assess renal function for contrast exposure

investigations.indication: Assess for pulmonary oedema, alternative diagnoses
investigations.expected_result: Likely normal given no clinical signs of heart failure

investigations.indication: Assess left ventricular function and wall motion abnormalities
investigations.expected_result: Inferior wall hypokinesis/akinesis, possible RV involvement if RCA dominant

immediate.intervention: STEMI pathway activation - call cardiology registrar and catheter lab immediately
immediate.rationale: Door-to-balloon time target <90 minutes for optimal outcomes in STEMI

immediate.intervention: High-flow oxygen if SpO2 <94%, IV access, cardiac monitoring
immediate.rationale: Supportive care while preparing for primary PCI

immediate.intervention: Morphine 2.5-5mg IV for pain control if required
immediate.rationale: Symptom relief, but avoid masking ongoing ischaemia

medications.contraindications: Active bleeding, severe bleeding disorder, aspirin allergy

medications.indication: P2Y12 inhibition for dual antiplatelet therapy in ACS
medications.contraindications: Active bleeding, moderate/severe hepatic impairment, concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, severe bradycardia, severe asthma
Active bleeding, severe bleeding disorder, recent surgery

learning_objectives: Apply systematic ECG interpretation methodology to identify STEMI
Recognize inferior STEMI pattern and understand coronary anatomy correlation
Implement evidence-based acute STEMI management protocols
Apply Australian guideline recommendations for primary PCI pathway

assessment_criteria.criteria: Systematic approach, correct identification of ST elevation in inferior leads, recognition of reciprocal changes, accurate measurements
Correlation of ECG findings with clinical presentation, understanding of coronary anatomy, risk stratification
Appropriate activation of STEMI pathway, correct medication choices with doses, contraindication awareness
Clear explanation of findings, appropriate urgency, patient counselling skills

key_teaching_points: Inferior STEMI typically involves RCA occlusion - leads II, III, aVF show ST elevation with reciprocal changes in I, aVL
Primary PCI is preferred reperfusion strategy if available within 90 minutes of first medical contact
Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) is cornerstone of medical management in ACS
Door-to-balloon time <90 minutes is quality indicator for STEMI care in Australian hospitals
common_mistakes: Failing to use systematic ECG interpretation approach and missing subtle reciprocal changes
Confusing inferior STEMI with posterior STEMI (which shows tall R waves in V1-V3)
Forgetting to check for contraindications to dual antiplatelet therapy before administration
Delaying STEMI pathway activation while waiting for troponin results - ECG diagnosis is sufficient
equipment_required: Calipers for precise ST segment measurement
ECG reference ranges and normal values chart
